  1. com.sbancuz.offscreen.api

Window API recipes

Choose Java, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, or ZenScript to create a screen and open it in a desktop window. The first examples show local controls and closing; later ones add custom drawing or connect controls to the server. All window operations run on Minecraft’s client thread.

Where the code runs

Java, Kotlin, Groovy and native Scala 3 can use the complete Java API, including HostUI adapters, scopes, ModularUI factories and HEI integration. Kotlin helpers use your Kotlin runtime; Scala helpers require native Scalar for Scala 3, not Scalar Legacy. GroovyScript exposes mods.offscreencleanroom.windows with reload-owned windows. CraftTweaker uses explicitly registered ZenScript types; its common-side screen declarations do not allocate native windows. GUI operations and callbacks run on Minecraft’s main client thread after initialization.

Imports below belong in client-only classes or client scripts. Native window creation needs Minecraft’s initialized graphics context. For CraftTweaker, put declarations in a #side client startup script and open them from an actual GUI/input action, not while loading the script. Restart after changing ordinary CraftTweaker 1.12 scripts.

Create a local screen

This defines screen content without opening a desktop window. The native examples extend Minecraft’s GuiScreen; the ZenScript version describes the same static content.

import net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen;
public final class HelloScreen extends GuiScreen {
    @Override public void drawScreen(int x, int y, float partialTicks) {
        drawRect(0, 0, width, height, 0xFF17232D);
        drawCenteredString(fontRenderer, "Hello", width / 2, 24, 0xFFFFFF);
        super.drawScreen(x, y, partialTicks);
    }
}

import net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen
class HelloScreen : GuiScreen() {
    override fun drawScreen(x: Int, y: Int, partialTicks: Float) {
        drawRect(0, 0, width, height, 0xFF17232D.toInt())
        drawCenteredString(fontRenderer, "Hello", width / 2, 24, 0xFFFFFF)
        super.drawScreen(x, y, partialTicks)
    }
}

import net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen
class HelloScreen extends GuiScreen {
    @Override void drawScreen(int x, int y, float partialTicks) {
        drawRect(0, 0, width, height, 0xFF17232D as int)
        drawCenteredString(fontRenderer, 'Hello', (width / 2) as int, 24, 0xFFFFFF)
        super.drawScreen(x, y, partialTicks)
    }
}

import net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen
class HelloScreen extends GuiScreen:
  override def drawScreen(x: Int, y: Int, partialTicks: Float): Unit =
    net.minecraft.client.gui.Gui.drawRect(0, 0, width, height, 0xFF17232D)
    drawCenteredString(fontRenderer, "Hello", width / 2, 24, 0xFFFFFF)
    super.drawScreen(x, y, partialTicks)

import mods.offscreencleanroom.Windows;
val hello = Windows.screen("Hello", 640, 480).background(-15260883);
hello.text("Hello", 24, 24, -1);

Coordinates inside a hosted screen are Minecraft GUI units. Window sizes are logical desktop units and may differ on scaled displays. Each open needs a fresh backing screen; a screen declaration can be reused.

Open a window, change its title, and close it

With the screen defined, open it from a client action and retain its window handle.

The opening code shows the screen in a desktop window, then sets its title and dimensions. Run it from a client button or key action and save the returned window. The final close call is a separate, later action: call it when the user finishes or when your controller is shutting down.

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI;
var window = OffscreenAPI.open(HelloScreen::new);
if (OffscreenAPI.isOpen(window)) {
    window.setTitle("Tools");
    window.resize(960, 640);
    window.setClearColor(0xFF17232D);
}
// Later, from the client thread:
OffscreenAPI.close(window);

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.*
val window = openWindow("Tools", 960, 640) { HelloScreen() }
window.setClearColor(0xFF17232D.toInt())
// Later, from the client thread:
OffscreenAPI.close(window)

def windows = mods.offscreencleanroom.windows
def window = windows.open({ new HelloScreen() }, 'Tools', 960, 640)
windows.configure(window) { current -> current.setClearColor(0xFF17232D as int) }
// Later; reload also closes only this registry's windows:
windows.close(window)

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.scaladsl.Offscreen.*
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI
val window = open("Tools", 960, 640)(new HelloScreen)
window.setClearColor(0xFF17232D)
// Later, from the client thread:
OffscreenAPI.close(window)

// Inside a client GUI/input callback, after declaring hello:
val window = hello.open();
window.title("Tools");
window.resize(960, 640);
window.clearColor(-15260883);
// Later, while retaining this exact handle:
window.close();

Closing releases this window’s adapters and synchronized session. Avoid global OffscreenAPI.closeAll() in an addon teardown: it also closes other addons’ windows. Groovy and ZenScript facades close only their own contributions.

Open a child screen or replace the current screens

Once a window is open, navigation can reuse it instead of opening another desktop window.

Push opens a child screen in the same desktop window while keeping its parent available. Back closes that child and reveals the parent. Replacing the root discards all previous screens. Each newly opened screen needs a fresh connecting adapter; do not reuse one that a window has already disposed.

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI;
OffscreenAPI.push(window, HelloScreen::new);
boolean returned = OffscreenAPI.pop(window);
window.setUI(new VanillaUI(new HelloScreen()));
int depth = OffscreenAPI.getScreenDepth(window);

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.*
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
window.pushScreen { HelloScreen() }
val returned = OffscreenAPI.pop(window)
window.replaceScreen(HostUIFactory {
    screen -> VanillaUI(screen as HelloScreen)
}) {
    HelloScreen()
}
val depth = window.screenDepth

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
windows.push(window, { new HelloScreen() })
def returned = windows.back(window)
windows.replace(window, { new HelloScreen() }, { screen -> new VanillaUI(screen) })
def depth = window.getScreenDepth()

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.scaladsl.Offscreen.*
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
window.pushScreen(new HelloScreen)
val returned = OffscreenAPI.pop(window)
window.replaceScreen(screen => new VanillaUI(screen.asInstanceOf[HelloScreen]))(new HelloScreen)
val depth = window.getScreenDepth()

val child = Windows.screen("Details", 480, 320);
window.push(child);
val returned = window.back();
window.replace(Windows.screen("New root", 640, 480));
val depth = window.depth;

ZenScript’s Escape action returns to the parent, then closes at the root; a consumed key event can override it. Do not replace a synchronized factory root with a local screen: the server protocol owns that root.

Draw dynamic content and update logic

The same window can display changing data. Update that data during ticks and draw the current values each frame.

This example changes screen content as time passes and draws it in a desktop window. The update function runs on client ticks, while drawing runs at the window’s configured frame rate. A low background-window FPS slows drawing, not client updates or server ticks.

public final class CounterScreen extends net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen {
    private int ticks;
    @Override public void updateScreen() {
        ticks++;
    }
    @Override public void drawScreen(int x, int y, float partial) {
        drawString(fontRenderer, "Ticks: " + ticks, 12, 12, 0xFFFFFF);
        super.drawScreen(x, y, partial);
    }
    @Override public void onGuiClosed() { /* Release only this screen's resources. */ }
}

class CounterScreen : net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen() {
    private var ticks = 0
    override fun updateScreen() { ticks++ }
    override fun drawScreen(x: Int, y: Int, partial: Float) {
        drawString(fontRenderer, "Ticks: $ticks", 12, 12, 0xFFFFFF)
        super.drawScreen(x, y, partial)
    }
    override fun onGuiClosed() { /* Release this screen's resources. */ }
}

class CounterScreen extends net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen {
    int ticks
    @Override void updateScreen() { ticks++ }
    @Override void drawScreen(int x, int y, float partial) {
        drawString(fontRenderer, 'Ticks: ' + ticks, 12, 12, 0xFFFFFF)
        super.drawScreen(x, y, partial)
    }
    @Override void onGuiClosed() { /* Release this screen's resources. */ }
}

class CounterScreen extends net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen:
  private var ticks = 0
  override def updateScreen(): Unit = ticks += 1
  override def drawScreen(x: Int, y: Int, partial: Float): Unit =
    drawString(fontRenderer, s"Ticks: $ticks", 12, 12, 0xFFFFFF)
    super.drawScreen(x, y, partial)
  override def onGuiClosed(): Unit = () // Release this screen's resources.

var ticks as int = 0;
hello.on("tick", function(event) {
    ticks += 1; return false;
});
hello.on("draw", function(event) {
    event.rect(8, 8, event.width - 16, 32, -16777216);
    event.text("Ticks: " ~ ticks, 12, 12, -1, true);
    return false;
});
hello.on("close", function(event) {
    print("Screen released"); return false;
});

ZenScript draw callbacks run after static elements and before buttons/tooltips. Drawing methods expire as soon as the callback returns, even if it throws. A declaration’s captured variables are shared across opens; use separate declarations for independent script state.

Receive text, key-up and pointer input

Interactive content also needs input. Add handlers for typing, keys and pointer events alongside drawing.

Use these functions to react to typed text, released keys, mouse movement, and scrolling before the screen handles them normally. The script example handles text and scroll events itself while leaving normal button clicks available. Typed text can contain several characters; physical key codes are for shortcuts and navigation.

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.input.KeyEvent;
var adapter = new VanillaUI(new HelloScreen()) {
    @Override public void onTextInput(String text) {
        System.out.println(text);
    }
    @Override public void onKeyPressed(KeyEvent key) {
        System.out.println(key.keyCode() + ":" + key.pressed());
        super.onKeyPressed(key);
    }
    @Override public void onMouseScroll(int x,
        int y,
        int step) {
        System.out.println(step);
    }
};

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.input.KeyEvent
val adapter = object : VanillaUI(HelloScreen()) {
    override fun onTextInput(text: String) { println(text) }
    override fun onKeyPressed(key: KeyEvent) {
        println("${key.keyCode()}:${key.pressed()}")
        super.onKeyPressed(key)
    }
    override fun onMouseScroll(x: Int, y: Int, step: Int) { println(step) }
}

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.input.KeyEvent
class InputAdapter extends VanillaUI {
    InputAdapter(HelloScreen screen) { super(screen) }
    @Override void onTextInput(String text) { println(text) }
    @Override void onKeyPressed(KeyEvent key) {
        println(key.keyCode() + ':' + key.pressed())
        super.onKeyPressed(key)
    }
    @Override void onMouseScroll(int x, int y, int step) { println(step) }
}

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.input.KeyEvent
val adapter = new VanillaUI(new HelloScreen):
  override def onTextInput(text: String): Unit = println(text)
  override def onKeyPressed(key: KeyEvent): Unit =
    println(s"${key.keyCode()}:${key.pressed()}")
    super.onKeyPressed(key)
  override def onMouseScroll(x: Int, y: Int, step: Int): Unit = println(step)

hello.on("text", function(event) {
    print(event.text); return true;
});
hello.on("key", function(event) {
    print(event.code ~ ":" ~ event.pressed);
    return false;
});
hello.on("scroll", function(event) {
    print(event.code); return true;
});
hello.on("drag", function(event) {
    print(event.heldMillis); return true;
});

HostUI also has click, release, drag, hover, resize, update and disposal hooks. ZenScript accepts draw, resize, tick, close, key, text, click, release, drag and scroll. True consumes input before vanilla handling; lifecycle return values are ignored. Event coordinates are GUI units. Native polling uses SDL scancodes/button numbers; do not confuse them with callback key/button indices.

Connect a custom screen to a desktop window

If your addon already has a screen framework, connect its drawing and input methods to the window.

Use this when Offscreen does not recognize your screen type. Supply a function that connects one fresh screen to drawing, input, resizing and cleanup through HostUI. The function is called an adapter factory. The returned window takes responsibility for disposing that adapter after successful installation.

var window = com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.open(
    HelloScreen::new,
    screen -> new com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI((HelloScreen) screen));

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.*
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
val window = openWindow(HostUIFactory {
    screen -> VanillaUI(screen as HelloScreen)
}) {
    HelloScreen()
}

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
def window = windows.openAdapted({ new HelloScreen() },
    { screen -> new VanillaUI(screen) }, 'Adapted tools', 960, 640)

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.scaladsl.Offscreen.*
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.vanilla.VanillaUI
val window = adapted(screen => new VanillaUI(screen.asInstanceOf[HelloScreen]))(new HelloScreen)

// ZenScript uses its callback-backed adapter rather than importing arbitrary Java GUI types.
val screen = Windows.screen("Adapted tools", 960, 640);
screen.on("draw",
    function(event) {
    event.text("Custom GUI",
    12,
    12,
    -1,
    false); return false;
});
screen.on("text", function(event) {
    print(event.text); return true;
});
// Open screen from your client action:
val window = screen.open();

Java, Kotlin, Groovy and Scala can implement HostUI or register a HostUIFactory with UIRegistry. ZenScript cannot implement arbitrary unexposed Java interfaces; its screen callbacks provide the supported adapter bridge. Resource ownership still transfers to the window on successful installation.

Open a screen whose controls update the server

For controls that change server-owned data, use a synchronized panel rather than a local screen.

The counter panel in this example sends button actions to the server and displays the returned value. First register an OffscreenSimpleFactory with the same name, handlers and registration order on both client and server. Keep that object for opening the panel later; in these snippets it is named factory. ZenScript finds it by its registered name.

var window = factory.openOffscreen();
if (com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.isOpen(window)) window.setTitle("Synchronized tools");
// Later:
com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.close(window);

val window = factory.openOffscreen()
if (com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.isOpen(window)) window?.setTitle("Synchronized tools")
// Later:
com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.close(window)

def window = factory.openOffscreen()
if (com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.isOpen(window)) window.setTitle('Synchronized tools')
// A direct Java factory call is owned by your controller, not the windows facade:
com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.close(window)

val window = factory.openOffscreen()
if com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.isOpen(window) then window.setTitle("Synchronized tools")
// Later:
com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI.close(window)

// Use an actual OffscreenSimpleFactory name registered by your addon on both sides.
val window = Windows.openSynchronized("my_addon_tools");
if (window != null) window.title("Synchronized tools");
// Later, close through this handle to release its server session:
if (window != null) window.close();

A returned window may still be waiting for the server to send its panel. ModularUI is required for these synchronized panels, but optional for local screens. HEI uses the same supported screen connections in every language. Minecraft still allows only one active slot container per player; opening another desktop window does not create an independent server inventory.

Kotlin and Scala helpers

Once the basic setup is in place, these helpers fit the same API into native language callbacks and result types.

Use Kotlin and Scala functions to open a window

Use popOutFunction when a callback API expects a Scala () => Unit or Kotlin () -> Unit. Keep popOutAction for Java Runnable callbacks. Both keep screen construction lazy and create a fresh screen on each invocation.

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.scaladsl.Offscreen.*
// Before: val action: Runnable = popOutAction(new MyScreen)
val action: () => Unit = popOutFunction(new MyScreen)
// Before: adapted(factory)(screen) may return null.
val window = adaptedOption(factory)(screen)
window.foreach(w => println(w))

adaptedOption returns None only when the shared API returns no window for a null screen or adapter. Native setup failures still propagate; a successful window remains owned by the caller. Kotlin's explicit-adapter openWindow(factory) { screen } already returns Window?. Invoke these actions on the client thread after graphics initialization; declaring a function does not open a window.

Calls used in the examples

Calls used in this guide
Call or settingArgumentsWhat it does
OffscreenAPI.open(screenFactory)Function creating a fresh screenJava, Kotlin, Scala and Groovy can call the same Java API directly.
popOutFunction / popOutActionScreen factory and the options shown belowChoose a native function for Kotlin/Scala callbacks, or an action for a Java Runnable. Screen creation stays lazy until invocation.
adaptedOptionScreen and adapter factoriesScala returns None for a missing screen or adapter; setup exceptions still propagate.

When you finish: Retain each returned window and close it from client teardown. Install the runtime for the chosen language; install CraftTweaker only for ZenScript. GUI callbacks run on the client thread. Declaring a callback must not open a screen.
